scenarios.title: insert `capacity` distinct keys into an empty cache
notes: One batch is one cold fill. The clear that makes it repeatable runs outside the timed region, so no adapter is charged for emptying itself.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: read a key that is present
notes: Random reads over the resident set. Map does no bookkeeping; QuickLRU promotes on every hit; blaze sets SIEVE’s visited bit — each library paying what its policy requires.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: read a key that was never written
notes: The cache is full but every read comes from a disjoint namespace — all three pay for a lookup that finds nothing.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: 90% reads / 10% writes under capacity pressure
notes: The control for `full-featured`: same load plan, no deadline and no tags on the writes.
Reads from a hot half, writes to a cold half of a `2 × capacity` key space, so the bounded caches evict continuously while Map keeps everything.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: the same load, with TTL and tags on every write
notes: The headline: what does a bounded, expiring, tag-invalidatable cache cost?
Identical to `mixed-90-10` except each write carries a one-hour deadline and one of 32 tags, and a tag is retired every 2500 iterations.
Map is given a hand-written LRU, deadline and tag index; QuickLRU supplies its own LRU and `maxAge` and is wrapped only for tags; blaze does all three in wasm.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: TTL-expiry-heavy churn: every read reclaims a lapsed entry
notes: Each untimed batch fills the cache with 1 ms deadlines and lets them lapse; the timed reads then do the lazy reclamation a synchronous cache must perform on access.
The two rivals expire with a hand-rolled deadline check and QuickLRU’s native `maxAge` respectively; blaze reclaims inside the Rust core and reports the drop through its log.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: a full cache evicts on every write
notes: Each batch is one full-cache fill followed by `capacity` writes to a disjoint namespace, so every single write has to reclaim a slot.
All three adapters are bounded here (Map + a hand-rolled LRU, QuickLRU, blaze): an unbounded Map would be doing strictly less work and its row belongs in the diagnostic table only.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: invalidation across a large tag index
notes: A full cache spread over 128 tags, retired every 200 iterations against a background of reads — the index, not the individual delete, is under test.
The hand-rolled mirror keeps both key→tags and tag→keys in step, including on eviction; blaze maintains both indexes in wasm.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: flush a full cache of dirty records to storage
notes: One timed op is a whole `capacity`-record flush; `ns/op` is normalised to **per record** so it can be read beside the point operations.

blaze uses its real write-through layer (debounce + reconciliation + one batched write) over an in-memory `CachePersistence`; the rivals use a hand-rolled pending-write queue over the same store. Node has no IndexedDB; the browser workspace runs the same scenario against real IDB-backed storage.
payload tiny/object

scenarios.title: restore a full cache from storage
notes: One timed op restores `capacity` stored records into a cleared cache; `ns/op` is per restored record.
Storage is seeded directly (bypassing the write path) so the number measures hydration alone. blaze uses `cache.persistence.hydrate()`; the rivals read the same rows and repopulate their stores.
payload tiny/object
